title: Late-loop field notes: Maia Chen — Runtime Architect loop
content:
Context / purpose:
- Quick internal notes from final loop for Maia Chen (candidate for Runtime Architect / Sr. MLE). Late loop ended 2026-02-09. This is my gut + evidence for hiring calibration and follow-ups.

Candidate quick summary:
- Background: 7+ years infra+ML. Last 3 years focused on inference optimizations at a mid-size infra startup (shipped KV cache + async batching). Strong C++ + Python, some CUDA exposure but not a kernel author. Good product sense for degradation strategies.
- Role fit hypothesis: can own performance features (KV caching, routing fallbacks, quantization choices) and drive production rollouts. Potential IC4/IC5 depending on deep ops experience.

Interview sequence / artifacts reviewed:
- Take-home: light microbenchmark harness + design doc (link above). They implemented a prototype that demonstrates prefix caching and a simple cache eviction policy. Code style rough but functional.
- Live system-design: design an inference stack for multimodal model with latency SLOs, explain routing + fallback.
- Live coding: implement a simplified LRU cache (JS-like pseudocode) and reason about concurrent access.

What I liked / evidence:
- Practical tradeoffs: explicitly called out interaction between KV cache and batching. Gave 3 concrete scenarios where caching hurts (hot keys causing head-of-line blocking, cache staleness after model update, memory blowouts with variable seq lengths) and proposed mitigations (per-client caps, versioned cache entries, size tiers).
- Take-home measured some perf numbers (p50/p99) and included a small script to simulate mixed request sizes — shows good quantitative thinking.
- Communication: concise, draws diagrams when thinking aloud. Good ability to prioritize (SLO vs cost).

Concerns / gaps observed:
- Kernel-level experience: limited. When pushed on kernel choices for quantized matmuls they deferred to team-level decision. Not a dealbreaker for a role that works with kernel teams, but matters if we expect them to author low-level kernels.
- Concurrency correctness: live coding produced a mostly-correct LRU, but missed corner-case reentrancy when multiple threads update size accounting; acknowledged quickly but fix was a bit hand-wavy. Would prefer to see a small unit test proving fix.
- No previous public OSS history of GPU kernels or Triton kernels; they have internal patches at prior company (can't review).

Detailed notes from segments:
- Take-home (score 7.5/10):
  - Positive: reproducible harness, clear README, measured perf, simple CLI for toggling cache modes.
  - Negatives: brittle test harness (hardcoded paths), could use more automated tests for correctness of eviction under pressure.
  - Follow-up ask: request unit test showing eviction under concurrent inserts (I asked them to add but timeboxed).

- System design (score 8/10):
  - Good separation of concerns: routing, batching, model variants, cache.
  - Nice fallback flow: route by latency floor -> if overloaded, fallback to smaller quantized variant or CPU-serving. Liked their SLO degradation policy (graceful ramp-down + per-tenant throttles).
  - Missing: deeper discussion on multi-tenant isolation for caching layer (how to prevent one noisy tenant from evicting others). They proposed per-tenant quotas but didn't flesh out eviction heuristics across tenants.

- Live coding (score 6.5/10):
  - Implemented main LRU operations quickly, clear variable names.
  - Missed atomicity on size updates; after hinting they proposed locks but not a lock-free sketch.
  - Would ask follow-up: how would you scale this LRU across multiple processes (shared-memory vs sharded local caches)? Their answer favored sharding by tenant key; fine but lacks discussion on cross-shard coherence.

Behavioral / culture fit:
- Teamwork: plenty of examples of cross-functional work with infra and model teams. Good at framing tradeoffs in terms dev effort vs impact.
- Drive: shipped features end-to-end at previous company, led a small team.
- Communication: persuasive in async write-ups (take-home doc was crisp).

Calibration vs our bar:
- For IC4 (senior engineer) checklist: strong systems thinking, shipping experience, good communication. Meets majority of criteria.
- For IC5 (staff): expect deeper kernel/quantization knowledge, stronger track record of shipping infra primitives that others depend on (TL;DR: borderline).

Suggested hiring levers / decision options:
- Option A: Hire at IC4 (strong hire). Rationale: immediate impact on caching+batching features, good safety with staff mentorship for kernel choices.
- Option B: Hire at IC5 (stretch hire) only if we get evidence of kernel-level contribution (OSS patches, deeper interview focused on quant kernels).
- Option C: No hire — only if concerns about concurrency correctness + kernel gap are red flags during calibration. Not my pick.

Recommended next steps (my preference = Option A):
1) Ask candidate to add one quick unit test in take-home showing eviction under concurrent inserts — 1-hour ask. If they deliver, move to offer.
2) Optional deep-dive: 60-minute kernel/quantization session with a staff engineer (not blocking, but will help calibrate level).
3) Compensation band: target IC4 band. Suggested base band: $180k–$210k (US comp bands) + equity typical for IC4. Note: adjust by local region.

Unresolved / open questions for hiring committee:
- Confirm willingness to accept IC4 vs IC5 title — candidate indicated preference for impact over title, but needs concrete expectations for kernel work.
- How much mentorship bandwidth do we have for someone who will need to collaborate with low-level kernel owners? (ask SRE/Platform leads).

Action items (me):
- Post this note to thread #recruiting-infra with draft recommendation.
- Send 1-hour test ask to Maia (unit test for eviction) and give 72-hour window.
- If test passes, draft offer package and loop in People Ops.

Random quick thoughts (brain dump):
- Might be useful to give them a short pairing session on an internal perf regression bug to see how they approach infra debugging.
- If we hire, pair them initially with Anais for 6 weeks on caching rollout (mentorship + knowledge transfer).

Bottom line (one line): Strong IC4 candidate — hire with a light verification test for concurrency correctness; escalate to IC5 only with additional kernel evidence.
